action_criteria.rationale: The outside CT after her fall reported enlarged ventricles only; MRI must measure the markers and exclude an obstructing lesion or subdural collection.

action_criteria.label: CSF tap test: opening pressure, routine CSF and removal of 30-50 mL

action_criteria.rationale: Repeating her unaided TUG and 10-m walk at 2 and 24 hours after the 40 mL tap shows whether her gait and freezing respond to CSF removal.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform the large-volume lumbar tap before brain MRI has excluded a mass or obstructive hydrocephalus

Do not diagnose iNPH from ventriculomegaly alone: the diagnosis needs the clinical syndrome (gait disturbance with cognitive or urinary symptoms) and supportive imaging, with no other cause explaining them [Relkin_2005]
Do not attribute the gait and cognitive decline to hypothyroidism when thyroid function is normal on replacement
Do not attribute the syndrome to normal ageing or deconditioning in a patient with ventriculomegaly, DESH and an objective tap response
required_recommendations: Refer to neurosurgery for CSF shunting with a programmable valve, on the basis of the tap-test improvement of 35% in TUG at 24 hours, the DESH MRI and normal-pressure CSF [Nakajima_2021]
Confirm euthyroid status (TSH 1.8 mIU/L, free T4 1.2 ng/dL) and continue levothyroxine 75 mcg unchanged
Falls-prevention measures (physiotherapy, home assessment, walking aid) while awaiting surgery

avoided_actions.rationale: She has had no seizures or fluctuating awareness, so an EEG does not address her progressive gait and cognitive syndrome.
Her falls happened while walking without loss of consciousness, so an ECG does not explain them.
She has no cardiac symptoms or embolic events, and an echocardiogram does not inform the iNPH work-up.
An outside CT already showed enlarged ventricles; MRI is available and measures the callosal angle, DESH and hippocampi better.
There is no syncope or palpitation history, so ambulatory rhythm monitoring has no diagnostic role.
Molecular or advanced imaging does not change the iNPH decision, which rests on MRI and the tap test.
A full neuropsychological battery is not needed for the iNPH decision; the bedside screen and timed gait measures are.
A two-year course without rapid decline, fever or inflammatory features gives no indication for prion, inflammatory or infectious CSF assays.

differential.diagnosis: Vascular cognitive impairment / subcortical ischaemic vascular disease
differential.key_features: Fazekas 1 white matter change without lacunes is too mild to explain her gait and cognition, which improve after CSF removal.
Freezing on initiation overlaps, but there is no tremor or rigidity and the wide-based gait improves after the tap.
Her mother had dementia of unknown cause, but gait came first, recall improves with cueing, MTA is 1 and the MoCA rises after the tap.
TSH 1.8 mIU/L and free T4 1.2 ng/dL on levothyroxine exclude undertreated hypothyroidism.

differential.diagnosis: Cerebral atrophy with secondary ex-vacuo ventriculomegaly
differential.key_features: Ventricles disproportionate to cortical volume loss, tight high-convexity sulci and an acute callosal angle argue against ex-vacuo enlargement.

differential.diagnosis: Secondary (post-traumatic, post-haemorrhagic or post-meningitic) communicating hydrocephalus
differential.key_features: Her only head injury, a minor contusion four months ago, came 20 months after the gait decline began, and the MRI shows no post-traumatic change.

key_clinical_evidence: Probable iNPH requires an insidious gait disturbance after age 40, progressing over at least 3 to 6 months without an antecedent cause, plus cognitive or urinary symptoms; she has all three over two years [Relkin_2005]
MRI shows Evans index 0.38 with both DESH components, a callosal angle of 73 degrees and temporal horn enlargement, with no obstructing lesion or subdural collection [Relkin_2005]
Opening pressure 13 cmH2O with normal CSF content meets the pressure criterion [Relkin_2005]
After removal of 40 mL, TUG fell from 26 to 17 s (35%) at 24 hours and the 10-m walk from 20 to 13 s; an improvement of 10% or more in TUG is a commonly used positive criterion [Nakajima_2021]
The tap test has a sensitivity of 26% to 61% and a PPV of 73% to 100%, so a clear response supports shunting while a negative tap would not have excluded it [Marmarou_2005]
Normal TSH and free T4 on levothyroxine exclude hypothyroidism as the cause of the syndrome

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Thyroid function is normal on replacement (TSH 1.8 mIU/L, free T4 1.2 ng/dL), so hypothyroidism does not explain the gait, urinary and cognitive syndrome.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Cognitive decline is attributed to hypothyroidism and a normal TSH is ignored

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The contusion was a consequence of the gait disorder, 20 months after it began, and the MRI shows no subdural collection or post-traumatic change, so it is not an antecedent cause.
red_herrings.data_point: Four months ago she struck her forehead in one of the falls
red_herrings.intended_effect: The hydrocephalus is attributed to head trauma and labelled secondary

sequence_constraints.reason: Brain imaging must exclude a mass or obstructive hydrocephalus before CSF is removed [Relkin_2005]
The baseline gait must be measured before the tap, or the post-tap change cannot be interpreted [Nakajima_2021]

patient.history_present_illness: A 72-year-old retired librarian with well-controlled hypothyroidism and hypertension was admitted for evaluation of a progressive two-year decline in gait, bladder function, and memory. She is a meticulous and organized person who is acutely aware of her functional decline. She first noticed a subtle change in her gait approximately two years ago, when her daughter noticed she was walking slowly and taking smaller steps than usual. Over the following year the gait impairment worsened substantially. She has fallen three times while walking (once in her kitchen, once at the post office, and once descending a curb), without loss of consciousness. She now uses a rollator walker for all outdoor ambulation and is very cautious indoors. She describes her feet as feeling 'stuck to the floor' when she tries to start walking. Her urinary symptoms began approximately 16 months ago with increasing urgency and episodes of leakage. She is embarrassed by the incontinence and has curtailed social activities. Her daughter has noted significant cognitive changes: she now forgets entire conversations from the previous day, has difficulty managing bills (previously did her own taxes), and becomes mildly confused when her routine is disrupted. She has been on levothyroxine for hypothyroidism for 12 years and reports consistent adherence. Her levothyroxine dose has not changed for over a year and her thyroid function has not been rechecked since. Her primary care physician attributed her symptoms to 'aging.' Four months ago she struck her forehead in one of the falls; a head CT obtained at an outside emergency department was reported as showing enlarged ventricles and no acute injury; the images are not available. Her primary care physician then referred her for progressive gait difficulty with memory decline and urinary urgency.
